ABSTRACT 12

Recent progress in methods used in the multiscale characterization of cementitious systems is reviewed, 13

focusing on advances in imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. The review includes relevant applications 14

and developments in machine learning and other data analytics approaches to enhance characterization. 15

Developments in imaging using light and electron microscopy as well as x-ray (i.e., from synchrotron) 16

methods are summarized. Updates include scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron 17

microscopy (TEM), tomography, and holography. A critical overview of spectroscopy (e.g., MAS NMR, 18

Raman) and scattering (e.g., neutron, x-ray, synchrotron x-ray) methods is provided, and the intersection 19

of these with imaging is developed (e.g., Raman imaging). Additionally, the paper summarizes recent 20

developments in and implementations of state-of-the-art machine-learning algorithms and data analytics 21

methods for automated, systematic, and/or quantitative analyses of image data sets. 22

The review considers but is not limited to the application of these methods for investigating the hydration 23

and microstructure development of cement phases, low-carbon-footprint cements (e.g., limestone calcined 24

clay cements, LC3), environmental interactions (e.g., ASR) and model systems. Thus, the present work 25

provides a critical presentation of advances in characterization methods that link together the composition 26

and multiscale structure of cementitious materials. 27

2.1.1 Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) 9

SEM has long been established as a tool for the microstructure investigation of cement materials. In 10

scanning electron microscopy (SEM), an image is obtained through the emission of electrons resulting from 11

a series of elastic and inelastic collisions with the interaction volume of the material. In high-energy SEM 12

(keV order), the incident electron beam is scanned over the sample's surface. The size of the interaction is 13

a few microns for the cementitious materials, composed of elements with a low atomic number. As a result 14

of the electron’s beam interaction with the volume of the materials, several types of signals are produced. 15

The most relevant ones for analytical purposes are the secondary electrons (SE), the backscattered electrons 16

(BSE), and the characteristic X-rays. SE images give information about the material's microstructure, 17

whereas BSE images are mainly used for elemental and phase quantification. The detection of 18

characteristics X-rays applied in energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS), or wavelength dispersive 19

spectrometry (WDS), is crucial for chemical/elemental analysis of the cement samples at a micron level. 20

Overall, the resolution of SEM is limited to 100-200 nm, although magnifications of up to 106x can be 21

achieved with modern instruments. This means that nanoscale features in calcium silicate hydrate phases, 22

ettringite and pores can be resolved [17], and recent advances in sample preparation and observation 23

techniques, described in this section, further improve the differentiation of fine nanostructural features by 24

SEM. Readers interested in SEM and chemical analysis fundamentals should refer to comprehensive 25

textbooks [18]. 26

27

Most papers published since the last ICCC (indicated in Figure 1(a)) used SEM-SE to inspect morphological 28

changes and chemical characterization through EDS point analysis. Some of the most relevant applications 29

of SEM in SE or BSE mode along with EDS analysis in cement science, include spatially resolved 30

investigations of phase composition such as C-(A)-S-H, spatially resolved compositions of complex 31

supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) [19] phase content estimations in hydrated cements, and 32

estimation of reaction degree [20,21]. 33

Most papers mentioned above used image analysis with grey-level segmentation of BSE images coupled 1

with EDS. Fully quantifiable spectral maps recorded for each pixel can be used to obtain the chemical and 2

spatial information of the microstructure. However, coupling SEM with EDS is challenging because the 3

characteristic size of most of the phases is much smaller than the EDS interaction volume. According to 4

[17], obtaining good feature resolution of calcium silicate hydrates (C-S-H) and other phases with BSE 5

down to 100-200 nm is possible. On the other hand, a clear distinction of different phases, such as ettringite, 6

remains challenging since ettringite precipitates in needles of less than 100 nm length compared to the 7

micrometer scale of the interaction volume [22]. Additionally, in complex systems such as OPC or LC3, 8

C-S-H is finely intermixed with ettringite, hydrotalcite, or other AFm phases, challenging phase 9

quantifications. 10

11

Some of these challenges have been addressed in recent years. For instance, Sui et al. [23] successfully 12

employed SEM-EDS analysis to study AFm solid solutions formed during chloride penetration in hydrated 13

Portland cement and Portland cement-limestone compositions. The average compositions of C-(A)-S-H 14

were determined through the Cl/Ca vs. Al/Ca ratios. This approach was further employed to estimate the 15

chloride physically bound to C-(A)-S-H. EDS was also used to confirm the presence of a solid solution 16

between Friedel’s salt and hemicarbonate for Portland cement-limestone samples exposed to chloride. 17

Another study carried out from Avet & Scrivener [24] used SEM-EDS and grey level in backscattered 18

electron imaging as tools for quantifying the gel water in the inner C-(A)-S-H in Portland cement and LC3 19

as a function of temperature variations over the range from 10 to 60 ºC. In the SEM-EDS approach, the 20

water was calculated from the difference of 100% and other element fractions (after deducing the oxygen 21

associated with the main detected elements). In the SEM-BSE approach, the water content of C-(A)-S-H 22

was calculated based on the changes in relative brightness, and the data were compared with the results 23

from TGA and 1H NMR. However, as pointed out by the authors, results obtained from the SEM-based 24

approach should be considered, at their best, an estimation of the water content as the errors are high as the 25

water content's determination depends on the other elements' accuracy. 26

In each of the above-mentioned studies, a considerable number of points per sample were used. For 28

instance, in the work of Sui et al. [23], an average of 8000 points per sample were used to investigate the 29

BSE-EDS maps. One of the major challenges when using these maps is the large amount of information 30

provided, and the user should carefully select the data from which a meaningful quantification can be 31

obtained. Another major limitation of SEM mapping is the required amount of time. For an experienced 32

user, 15-20 hours of work may be necessary for preparing one sample and analysis in the microscope, 33

including acquiring and quantifying these maps. In this regard, a new approach that allows for the phase 34

separation, chemical analysis, and visualization of the BSE images was presented by Georget et al. [22]. 35

The approach is based on the combination of four main steps involving (i) denoising and combination into 36

composite maps from individual maps, (ii) segmentation and extraction of representative points from each 37

composite map through segmentation algorithms, (iii) identification of phases by ratio plots and (iv) 38

application of masks for phase identification in the whole microstructure. In the last step of the work, the 39

maps are created from the regions identified in the ratio plots, which are subsequently applied to identify 40

similar phases in the investigated area. This approach allows for a reproducible method to obtain ratio plots 41

from SEM-EDS hypermaps and relate these ratio plots to BSE images, thus leading to a clear and good 42

determination of mixed phases. The masks can be adopted depending on the type of sample. The method 43

was implemented into a new framework called ‘edxia’ and added as a plugin to the Glue graphical software 44

[25]. The authors demonstrated the framework's robustness by analyzing different AFm phases. An 45

example of the qualitative phase separation applying the edxia approach instead of EDS point analysis is 46

given in Fig. 2. 47

2.1.2 Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) 16

In contrast to SEM, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) allows for a far more local and precise sample 17

analysis. Two main modes of TEM are used in cement science; (i) traditional imaging, where the electron 18

beam is stationary, and the atoms of the prepared sample result in a high-resolution image from the 19

transmitted beam, and (ii) scanning mode, known as well as scanning transmission electron microscopy 20

(STEM) where the beam scans over the sample. The beam is focalized in a small probe area in the STEM 21

mode, allowing scanning through the surface. Similar to the case of SEM, TEM can be coupled with energy 22

dispersive spectrometry. Adsorption and fluorescence effects do not occur in TEM as the sample is very 23

thin. For a proper quantitative analysis, the sample must be tilted towards the EDS detector to avoid 24

generating unwanted X-rays from thick regions of the sample. In contrast to SEM, the TEM technique 25

offers a much higher spatial resolution of the sample, to just below 0.2nm, approaching atomic scale 26

resolution.  Single-digit nanoscale spatial resolution has been reported for hydrated C-S-H [add ref]. 27

Investigations to such high spatial resolution help to avoid phase intermixing, which may be problematic 28

for nanostructure investigation. A selected area electron diffraction (SAED) technique can also be applied 29

in TEM to assess whether the investigated phases are crystalline or amorphous. 30

3.1 MAS NMR spectroscopy 13

Nuclear magnetic resonance observes radio frequency signals from atomic nuclei occupancy excited spin 14

states, thus giving information on the investigated probe's atomic-scale structure and dynamical behavior. 15

The technique applied the most for investigations of solids is Magic Angle Spinning Nuclear Magnetic 16

Resonance, i.e., MAS NMR. The primary interaction for solids consists of (i) interaction of the dipole 17

moment of the observed nuclei with the dipole moment of other individual nuclei of some other species, 18

(ii) anisotropy of the shielding, and (iii) anisotropy of the electrical filed gradient causing quadrupole 19

interaction. MAS NMR reduces the peak broadening caused by these interactions by spinning the sample 20

around an axis oriented at 54.7º relative to the external magnetic field B0. MAS NMR represents a powerful 21

analytical tool that can be utilized for structural characterization. The main advantage of the technique is 22

that it allows the study of amorphous cementitious components such as C-(A)-S-H, thus complementing 23

other characterization techniques such as X-ray diffraction and thermal analysis. A considerable amount of 24

the information can be collected through 1H, 27Al, 29Si, or 25Mg, 43Ca spectra. The application of the 25

technique to cement science has a long history, as the first investigations on cement were carried out by 26

Lippmaa et.al [78] on hydrated tricalcium silicate utilizing 29Si MAS NMR for structural characterization 27

of C-S-H, followed by the work additional work [79–81] on 27Al MAS NMR on studies of calcium 28

aluminate cements and tricalcium aluminate phase. For a comprehensive summary of the earliest 29

applications of MAS NMR in cement science and an in-depth description of the background of the solid- 30

state NMR, the reader refers to more advanced [82] textbooks. Whereas a review summarizing applications 31

of solid-state NMR in understanding the chemistry and materials science of cement until 2019 was provided 32

by Walkley & Provis [83]. 33

4.3 Synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function (PDF) 7

Because XRD does not allow for a full investigation of gel phases, it must be coupled with other techniques 8

such as thermal analysis, MAS NMR or FTIR, or Raman spectroscopy to allow for a detailed investigation 9

of phase composition. X-ray and neutron pair distribution function (PDF) analysis are well-established 10

techniques that will probe the local atomic structure of gel phases [129]. Model systems based on hydrated 11

alite, belite, and ye’elemite-anhydrite systems were investigated through PDF to better understand 12

carbonation reactions [130]. The PDF study established that the carbonation of C-S-H/portlandite results in 13

three crystalline polymorphs of CaCO3, along with amorphous silica and other carbonates. Under 14

accelerated carbonation conditions, ye’elemite-anhydrite resulted in bassanite, aragonite, and gibbsite. In 15

addition, the local structure of C-S-H gel from the hydration of alite and silica fume was examined through 16

[131] synchrotron pair distribution function. The study revealed that the C-S-H formed by the pozzolanic 17

reaction has the same local structure as the primary C-S-H. In contrast, differential PDF indicates that 18

excess portlandite is present with a nanostructure of a few-layers thick (nanometer range) along the c-axis. 19

20

The characterization of multiphase complex systems through PDF, remains extremely challenging as 21

summarized in the review paper from Shi et al. [132]. However, in-situ X-ray total scattering and PDF 22

analysis have been used to investigate the gel structure of alkali-activated materials. Most recently Gong & 23

White [133], presented an approach to quantity amorphous-crystalline transformations occurring in NaOH- 24

activated GGBS cured for five months by combining atomistic modeling with in-situ synchrotron PDF 25

analysis, thus highlighting the power of combining atomistic modeling and in-situ X-ray PDF analysis to 26

model the reaction mechanism in complex systems. The structural representation of amorphous slag 27

components was generated through force field-based molecular dynamics (MD) and validated using X-ray 28

PDF data along with other structural hydrate phases (obtained from literature), thus allowing phase 29

quantification over time and, most importantly, quantification of the overall degree of reaction (DOR) over 30

time. A good agreement was obtained from the presented approach and literature, whereas the real in-situ 31

space PDF-derived DOR was validated by FTIR analysis and quasi-elastic-neutron scattering. In an 32

additional work [134] MD simulations with density functional theory (DFT) were combined to generate a 33

structural representation of CaO-MgO-Al2O3-SiO2 (CMAS) glasses. The simulations were validated 34

through experimental synchrotron X-ray and neutron total scattering data. A correct assignment of the atom- 35

atom correlation in the medium range (around 3-8 Ǻ) order was achieved. A consistent agreement was 36

found between literature data on aluminosilicates concerning interatomic distances, coordination numbers, 37

oxygen environments, and angular distribution. Figure 18 represents a visualization of the structural 38

5 Machine learning for microstructural characterization of cementitious materials 13

The use of machine learning (ML) techniques as computer vision methods is a rapidly growing field of 14

study, with numerous direct applications in the advanced image-based characterization of cementitious 15

materials.  Recent applications in 2D imaging, 3D imaging, and in-situ 3D /4D imaging are reviewed. 16

5.1 ML applied to 2D imaging 18

Machine learning-based classification, object detection, segmentation, and clustering models can be 19

directly applied in 2D imaging-based characterization. For image classification tasks, deep convolutional 20

neural network (CNN) models were used on 2D BSE-SEM images to classify different types of cement 21

composites (e.g., OPC and graphene oxide-silica) and provide embedded image features from models to 22

characterize the distribution of microstructure [135,136]. In addition, CNN models were utilized to classify 23

cement paste mixtures with different water-to-cement ratios and silica fume dosage based on SEM images. 24

The classification performance was improved with transfer learning [137]. For object detection tasks, deep 25

CNN models (e.g., Mask R-CNN model [138], path aggregation network (PANet) model [139] were 26

applied to detect air-voids on microscopy images with bounding boxes combined with probability (Fig. 19). 27

For phase segmentation tasks, both classical machine learning models (e.g., random forest, SVM, KNN, 4

machine learning models in 3D/ in-situ 3D tomography image analysis will be discussed in detail. 10

Unsupervised clustering modes like k-means were also applied on SEM images to segment different phases 11

emission (AE) images, clustering methods (e.g., k-means [146], self-organizing map (SOM) [147], 13

provided labels, were coupled with support vector machine (SVM) classification model to classify crack 14

modes at a macro-scale. 15

Machine learning models have been widely applied in the 2D image based microstructural characterization 16

of cementitious materials with high accuracy and automation. The needs and work for human annotations 17

are low considering the small size of data for 2D images and the assistance from unsupervised labelling 18

5.2 ML applied to 3D imaging 26

Systematically investigating the microstructure of cementitious material requires three-dimensional image 27

processing (e.g., tomography (CT)), segmentation of different components (phases), characterization of the 28

morphological characteristics, and c statistical analysis. Traditional methods for image processing, such as 29

segmentation and analysis, involve manual and intentional processes, which are slow, inaccurate, and non- 30

reproducible. Besides, the large amount (hundreds of GB per sample) of volumetric data requires new 1

developments in image processing [58]. Emerging algorithms addressing large and complex datasets and 2

data analysis methods, emphasizing pattern recognition and machine learning [148], provide new 3

opportunities to develop computer-vision-based image processing to meet these challenges. The advanced 4

algorithms and prototype software can quantify the structure, distribution, orientation, and connectivity of 5

various phases (e.g., pore, aggregate, hydration product, crack, and fiber) in concrete and cement samples 6

based on 3D images. 7

Both classical machine learning models (e.g., support vector machines (SVM) [149], logistic regression 8

[150] random forest [151] [149] and deep learning models (artificial neural network [151], U-Net [152,153] 9

, Deeplab [153,154], modified ResNet [153], as computer vision methods, have been successfully applied 10

to segmented different phases (i.e., void, crack, steel fiber, PVA fiber, aggregate, matrix, etc.) in 3D 11

tomographic images of cementitious materials (Fig. 20). Morphological quantification and mechanical 12

analysis have been conducted based on segmented 3D phase images (Fig. 21). For example, pore size 13

distribution [144] [151], aggregate distribution [154], fiber orientation [151][155] and crack 14

distribution[153] from 3D images under mechanical and environmental loading have been characterized. 15

In addition, segmented 3D phase images have been utilized for 3D concrete modelling. However, one of 16

the challenges for 3D image segmentation using the above-supervised learning methods is data labelling. 17

To achieve high-performance phase segmentation results, a large number of high-quality annotated images 18

are required, which cannot be well-handled by traditional manual labelling. To solve this, a semi-automatic 19

labelling method has been proposed, combining k-means clustering to divide the 2D cement tomographic 20

image into multiple clusters with manual correction (detailed explanation with flowchart is in Figure 22). 21

This approach improved the quality of training data; the accuracy of the segmentation model, and the 22

efficiency of the overall data analysis pipeline [154]. 23

Currently, most applications focus on 3D images from X-ray tomography. Similar models and pipelines 24

can be applied to processing other advanced 3D imaging methods (e.g., neutron tomography, FIB-SEM) 25

with only minor modifications. Further, there is a potential to use the 3D U-Net model [156] in 3D image 26

analysis, accelerated by GPU and distributed computation, to improve performances in both accuracy and 27

efficiency significantly. 28

5.3 ML applied to in-situ 3D imaging: 1

Advances in in-situ tomography tests allow scanning of the internal 3D microstructures of the cementitious 2

materials over time, including under progressive loading at each load steps or environmental exposure at 3

each time step. Characterizing micro-level of phase evolution is critical in understanding the mechanism 4

during in-situ hydration, testing or exposure. Similar machine learning and deep learning models, as 5

mentioned in the prior 3D imaging section, can be used in the processing of in-situ 3D images directly. 6

However, the additional time axis increases the size of the raw data. For example, in high-resolution 7

microtomography, data sets can be at the level of TB per experiment. 8

Therefore, an autonomous and accurate in-situ tomography image analysis is required. Xu et al. [157] 9

proposed a machine learning-based in-situ 3D phase segmentation and analysis approach (Fig. 23), which 10

combines other image-based characterization method (e.g., SEM) and advanced digital volume correlation 11

(DVC) to investigate mechanical responses systematically (e.g., stress/strain and fracture pattern (Fig. 24)), 12

phase information (e.g., pore, aggregate and fiber (Fig. 25)) [155][157] and durability properties ( including 13

water transport properties) [58]. Note that digital volume correlation (DVC) technique maps the relative 14

deformation and tracks the sub volumes between consecutive tomography images, which is an appropriate 15

image processing method for the in-situ 3D tomography images. The bulk mechanical properties (i.e., strain 16

fields) and fracture mechanisms can be calculated from the displacement fields; further, the crack 17

propagations can be visualized. The combination of in-situ 3D phase (e.g., aggregates) and DVC improved 18

the accuracy of 3D kinematical fields (i.e., displacement and strain) characterization, [150] [152]. Also, 19

integrated in-situ synchrotron X-ray tomography and in-situ neutron radiography with machine learning- 20

based computer vision analysis is a powerful non-destructive testing method for systematically 21

investigating the complex concrete microstructure, including examination of the dynamics of water 22

penetration [58]. 23

6 Concluding remarks 6

Understanding and modelling the complexity of cementitious systems on a fundamental basis remains a 7

challenging task, although it is of vital importance for advancement of concrete technology. The current 8

work reviews recent advancements of some of the major direct and indirect characterization techniques 9

applied for the investigation of hydrated cementitious systems. In particular, this review placed emphasis 10

on innovations in sample preparation, characterization environment or approach, and applications of 11

machine-learning algorithms and data analytics methods for automated, systematic, and/or quantitative 12

analyses of image data sets. Further, this review demonstrated that improving fundamental understanding 13

of single phase and Portland cement hydration remains important, as does characterization of environmental 14

degradation of cementitious materials and the products of that degradation. As well, this review found 15

contributions in the characterization of the hydration of phases in alternative cements and their phases (e.g., 16

ye’elemite) and in complex systems (e.g., LC3), showing the growing interest in innovating cement 17

compositions to meet sustainability goals. The continued increasing rate of scholarly productivity and 18

innovation since 2019, despite the challenges stemming from the pandemic during this period, demonstrate 19

the resiliency of the research community in this field. 20

21

Aside the improvement of the most established methods, i.e SEM and TEM, progress has been made in 22

utilization of the above techniques in a more automated manner. For instance, the edxia strategy has been 23

proposed as a new image analysis approach that allows for phase separation, chemical analysis and 24

visualization of different phases from SEM-EDS hypermaps using superpixel subsampling of a composite 25

map. Sample preparation strategies have been as well improving and the focus is slowly shifting toward the 26

application of additional techniques such as Argon BIB, FIB and Cryo, extending the utility of SEM and 27

TEM. Additionally, ptychography imaging has made major progress and several groups have employed 28

soft and hard X-ray ptychography to examine cement hydration as it allows for submicrometer spatial 29

resolution. High spatial resolution information from ptychography and in-situ microtomography when 30

coupled with in-situ synchrotron powder diffraction allows for the collection of changes in major phases 31

with volumetric data facilitating spatial mapping over hydration age. Since the last ICCC in 2019, more 32

insights have been gained into the local structure of C-(A)-S-H, and N-(A)-S-H specially by the application 1

of solid-state MAS NMR that provides for precise local structure on quadrupolar nuclei of complex phases 2

information if experiments are carried out at ultra-high magnetic fields. The application of in-situ MAS 3

NMR and Raman spectroscopy is becoming as well more commonly used in this field. 4

5

In the review presented at ICCC 2019 [15] machine learning was foreseen as a fundamental approach for 6

automated image analysis and quantification, the application of which could allow for a better design of 7

complex systems. Since then, extraordinary progress has been made in the application of machine learning 8

and computer vision for the analysis of microstructural evolution of cementitious materials. For instance, a 9

state-of-the-art machine-learning pipeline combined with digital volume correlation for automated 10

microtomography segmentation analysis has been developed and applied to in-situ synchrotron x-ray µCT 11

as a tool of characterization for the microstructure evolutions of strain-hardening cementitious composites. 12

This is a step forward to a precise quantitative understanding of damage evolution in cement microstructure, 13

likely leading to enhancements the predictive ability of existing micromechanics-based models 14

For the reader, it may become evident that the structural complexity of cementitious systems is such that 15

no unique tool can provide all the desired details. Therefore, many of the papers reviewed herein employed 16

a multimethod approach to advance the field. 17

## Abstract

Recent advances addressing the development of anti-mildew and UV-resistance microcapsules for wood.

IPBC is enclosed in the drug-loaded carriers, through slow release, resulting in the anti-mildew process.

Anti-mildew experiments showed that the control effectiveness of 1.25wt% nano SiO2-IPBC

microcapsules was 78.125% against Botryodiplodia theobromae. In addition, a novel angle of view is

discussed, which is the UV-resistance, including different mass fraction of nano SiO2-IPBC

microcapsules, IPBC and the control group. Different FTIR characterizations and surface color related to

impregnated wood samples are discussed. Nano SiO2-IPBC microcapsules had better bonding

performance and UV-resistance than IPBC due to the synergistic effect of nano SiO2 and IPBC in the

microcapsules. Color measurements showed that the UV-resistance of microcapsules was better than

1.25wt% IPBC impregnated wood samples.

It helps us open new horizons to anti-mould agent, which offers multi-function of great anti-mildew effect

and excellent UV-resistance. The simple and green method for the preparation of microcapsules would

have tremendous potential for the extensive development of wood protection.

## 1 Introduction

One of the most important methods for a wider utilization of the CO2-storing resource wood is to prevent

it from biological attack and UV-aging. Therefore, the anti-mildew feature and light stability of rubberwood is quite significant. Rubber wood (Hevea brasiliensis (Willd. ex A. Juss.) Muell. Arg.) is widely

used in furniture, it is abundant of starch and sugar, which offers a great environment for various fungi and insects. And thus, the biological attack narrowed the application range and life of rubber wood.

(Wang et al. 2021). In general, anti-mold agents featured in green processes could effectively resist mold infestation on wood surfaces, such as IPBC, dodecyl dimethyl ammonium chloride, borates, and quaternary ammonium salts (Wu et al. 2021; Sanchez C L et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2011; Liu et al. 2018).

However, they are susceptible to leaching and loss when applied in humid environments, resulting in greatly reduced anti-mildew efficiency (Zhang et al. 2020). Therefore, developing an environment-friendly

with excellent biocompatibility anti-mold agent is a challenge in the field of wood mildew-proofing.

Color and color stability are important features of products made from wood (Tolvaj and Mitsui 2005). When the wood surface is exposed outdoors or to ultraviolet light source indoors, it could lead to wood

photoaging. This is due to the serious photooxidation and degradation of wood surface under ultraviolet radiation. (Li 2003). The aromatic polymer lignin is the wood constituent most sensitive to UV light, which

absorbs 80–95% of the UV radiation striking the wood. (Xie et al. 2005) UV light contain enough energy to break chemical bonds in lignin creating aromatic free radicals and other radicals (Kataoka et al. 2007,

Zhang et al. 2009). Free radicals can further degrade cellulosic components of wood cell walls through chemical reactions, which lead to the formation of colored quinone-like components (Muller et al. 2003,

Guo et al. 2016). The fragmentation of lignin exposes the underlying cell wall structure and leads to further degradation of the surface, which is then more prone to fungal attack (Hernandez and Evans


<!-- Page 3 -->


Page 3/25

2015). Therefore, it is of great importance to use anti-mildew treatments to extend the life of rubber wood by increasing anti-mildew ability as well as resistance to UV irradiation (Lebow et al. 2010).

Traditionally, coatings represent the easiest and most common method for protecting wood from UV radiation and biological attack. However, some coatings require the high curing temperature to obtain the

protective coating, the wood properties would be damaged under the desired temperature (Zayat et al., 2007). Opaque coatings such as paint totally mask the natural texture of wood, which could not meet the

purpose of maintaining the natural wood appearance. Clear varnishes allow the natural figure and grain of wood to-be seen, but the UV light could penetrate and photodegrade the wood underneath (MacLeod et

al. 1995). UV absorbers (Bisht et al. 2021) and hindered amine light stabilizers (Hodgson and Coote 2010) in clear coatings can restrict the amount of UV radiation that reaches the wood surface and

improve coating longevity, but the matrix degradation, dispersions of UV-absorbing molecules in polymer matrices exhibit low photostability upon prolonged irradiation with UV light (Macleod et al. 1995; Panek

and Reinpreht 2014). Therefore, clear coatings could only provide short-term protection when exposed under ultraviolet radiation. (Evans et al. 2015) The desired agent needs to penetrate into the wood

substrate to the required depths and meet the necessary retention levels. (Currie et al. 2021). One alternative to the use of traditional surface protection treatments is the use of nano particles. Nano

particles can be readily dispersed in the solution without major additives, and the large surface to volume ratios endow them with many unique characteristics including the ability to move through into the

internal wood and higher resistance to leaching than big molecules (Bak 2018). In addition, wood can be an excellent matrix material because of its porous and skeletal structure, which can absorb and

mechanically support inorganic nanomaterials. Inorganic nanoparticles are accepted as more stable and safe anti-UV agents. (Bai et al. 2017) As a result, the combination of inorganic nano-materials and wood

can provide overall better performance of the wood.

Microencapsulation is a significant technology used for long-term preservation of functional processes,

which can be used in drug delivery and controlled release. Microencapsulation technology offers many possibilities for improving the properties of wood, or it can endow them completely new functions. In

microencapsulation, a number of different materials can be utilized in order to improve its own defects and elaborate its proper effect. Liu and Xu (2019) used MUF to prepare a wood microcapsule

preservative, and the results showed that the microcapsule preservative from neem extract was more stable than the neem extract preservative. Shao et al. reported a spray-drying microencapsulation, the

microcapsules had good surface morphology and retaining 50% the active constituent after 10 weeks of

storage (Shao et al.,2019). In addition, microcapsules could offer sustained release of herbicides instead of high doses of the chemicals to agricultural land (Cao et al. 2019).

Nano SiO2 particles showed high absorbance in UV region, which can be used as UV-shielding

applications. (Hashim and Hamad 2020). Due to Nazir, nano SiO2 offered 3 times UV shielding

performance more than the micro SiO2 (Nazir and Phung 2018). In addition, nano SiO2 particles have

become a research hotspot because of its simple preparation process, eco-friendliness, good biocompatibility and high loading capacity (Manzano & Vallet-Regí 2020; Gao et al. 2020). However, in

### 2.1 Experimental materials

Rubber wood with the age of 20 were cut from the Experimental Forest of Chinese Academy of Tropical Agricultural Sciences. Clear air-dried wood samples with the water content about 15% were prepared with the size of [20 mm(L)×10 mm(R) ×5mm (T)]. The prepared samples were stored in a self-sealing at the

temperature of -18℃ in order to prevent fungal infection (GB/T 18261—2013).

Absolute ethanol, cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), ammonia, 3- iodo-2-propynylbutylcarbamate (IPBC). The above analytical purity was purchased from Macklin Reagent

Experimental strains: Botryodiplodia theobromae, Aspergillus niger, Trichoderma viride, Penicillium citrinum, which were purchased from China General Microbiological Culture Collection Center. 2.2 Preparation of SIM

Preparation of nano SiO 2 -IPBC microcapsules

Herein, soft-templating method is used due to its convenience and high efficiency via surfactant molecular self-assembly. Nano SiO2 particles were prepared as following: TEOS, CTAB, distilled water and

ammonia water are mixed in order in a molar ratio of 1:0.2:160:1.5. (Sun et al.2003). Wash the prepared mixture 3 times with distilled water, and then put it into the oven for 90℃ drying. After the solid was obtained, put it into a muffle furnace calcination for 5 hours at 600℃ to remove the CTAB template, so as

to obtain nano SiO2 particles. In order to load the IPBC molecules into the prepared nano SiO2 particles,

mix the prepared nano SiO2 particles and IPBC with 20% ethanol solution with ultrasonic dispersion

treatment for 20min, and vacuumed to -0.09MPa, 1 h for IPBC loading. And then centrifuge the resultant

## 4 Conclusion

In this study, we show that SIM can not only strengthen the anti-mold efficiency of IPBC and make it

deposit in the wood grain hole and conduit, but also decrease the yellowness of UV-aging problems of wood. Combined results from anti-mildew results, SEM and CIE color measurements show that the SIM

suppressed the attack of main fungi and helped prevent yellowness of wood. Future investigations are planned to examine approaches for the relationship between the degree of rubber wood ash change and

the adding amount of SIM, with the aim of keeping the original color of the wood and anti-mildew effect. In general, further study on the connection between the discoloration of wood samples and the content of

SIM are needed.

Abstract: Limestone (calcite) calcined clay cement (LC3) is a promising low-CO2 binder, but the 16

low activity of calcite cannot compensate the reduction in clinker factor, resulting in low one-day 17

strength and limiting its broad applications. As recent carbon capture and utilization technologies 18

allow scalable production of vaterite, a more reactive CaCO3 polymorph, we overcome the 19

challenge by introducing vaterite calcined clay cement (VC3), inspired by the vaterite-calcite 20

phase change. In the present study, VC3 exhibits higher compressive strengths and faster 21

hydration than LC3. Compared to hydrated LC3, hydrated VC3 exhibits increased amount of 22

hemi- and mono-carboaluminate formation and decreased amount of strätlingite formation. With 23

gypsum adjustment, the 1-day strength of VC3 is higher than that of pure cement reference. VC3, 24

a low-CO2 binder, presents great potential as a host of the metastable CaCO3 for carbon storage 25

and utilization and as an enabler of carbon capture at gigaton scales. 26

27

Keywords: carbon utilization; carbon storage; CCUS; bio-inspired; low-CO2 cement. 28

1.Introduction 30

Portland cement is the most versatile binder in construction, with current production of over 31

4 Gt/year and a projected increase in demand by 50% [1]. The massive cement production 32

accounts for ~8% of global anthropogenic CO2 emissions [2]. As the second largest commodity 33

after freshwater, the decarbonization of cement is of great interest but great challenges as well. 34

Gigaton-scale decarbonization by alternative or blended low-carbon cement is handicapped by 35

economic viability, technical feasibility, and scalability (e.g., raw materials distribution) [3]. 36

Most modern cement kilns are at or close to the maximum thermal efficiency [4]; thus, 37

decarbonization strategies have focused on exploring materials alternative or supplementary to 38

cement. The partial cement clinker replacement by supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs, 39

e.g., coal fly ash) is a mature cement decarbonization strategy [5]. However, due to the global 40

energy transition, in recent years, byproduct SCMs from other industries (e.g., fly ash from coal 41

power plants and granulated blast furnace slag from iron manufacturing) could not meet the 42

massive cement demand [6]. With the high natural reservoir capacity of limestone (calcite), 43

limestone calcined clay cement (LC3) has been widely validated as a scalable, low-cost solution 44

to cement decarbonization at a clinker content of up to 50% [7, 8]. Both limestone and clay are 45

locally available and massively sourced at low costs. LC3 with 50% clinker replacement can 46


<!-- Page 4 -->


2

achieve equivalent strengths to ordinary Portland cement by 3 days [9],exhibiting higher late-age 47

mechanical properties due to refined microstructure by reactions between clinker / hydrates, 48

limestone, and calcined clay (mainly metakaolin) [10]. Besides calcium aluminosilicate hydrate 49

(C-A-S-H), other major reaction products (i.e., hemicarboaluminate, monocarboaluminate, and 50

strätlingite) also play important roles in the enhanced durability of LC3 [11]. Requiring no special 51

handling or training, LC3 technology has been readily deployable at scale [12]. 52

Despite many advantages and industrial interests [13], LC3 presents unignorable limitations: 53

1) low early-age strengths (e.g., at 1 day) [14]; 2) complex rheology (e.g., poor flowability) [15]; 54

and 3) production slowdown due to enhanced needs for grinding specific components of LC3. 55

While inter-grinding clinker, gypsum, calcined clay, and limestone using mills does not reduce 56

the productivity of blended cement, the particle size distribution of each component of LC3 is 57

difficult to optimize and affects productivity. Thus, the common strategy, e.g., in the U.S. 58

markets, is instead inter-blending where Portland cement, calcined clay, and limestone are 59

individually ground to the required fineness and blended together [16], compromising the 60

production rate. 61

The low 1-day strength of LC3 may be mitigated by chloride-based [17] or calcium silicate 62

hydrate (C-S-H) seed-based accelerators [18]. However, using such accelerators limits the use of 63

LC3 concrete to non-reinforced applications or at low water-to-cement ratios [17, 19]. The 64

abovementioned limitations may be resolved simultaneously with the new ternary Portland 65

cement system – vaterite calcined clay cement (VC3), in which the limestone powders of LC3 are 66

replaced by vaterite, a metastable CaCO3 polymorph with a higher reactivity in Ca-rich 67

cementitious systems, compared to calcite [20]. Additionally, the spherical nature of vaterite 68

particles mitigates the flowability issue associated with LC3. Recent advances in the deployment 69

of climate technology (e.g., by Calera and Fortera) allow low-cost production of vaterite at scale 70

with co-benefits of air CO2 capture or point source carbon capture [21]. The global warming 71

potential of vaterite production through carbon storage depends on the carbon footprint of energy 72

use (e.g., renewable electricity), CO2 capture efficiency, raw materials, and type of processes. 73

Via the “climate tech” pioneers, the embodied carbon of vaterite production could be down to 74

0.3 kg CO2 per kg of vaterite produced, while stoichiometrically, 1 kg of vaterite can store 0.44 75

kg of CO2. Thus, vaterite can be potentially produced at an overall “negative” carbon 76

embodiment (i.e., -0.14 kg CO2/kg vaterite). 77

A proof-of-concept study is needed for the potential outperformance of VC3 over LC3. 78

Although VC3 is similar to LC3 at first glance, metastable vaterite may alter the chemistry and 79

microstructure of the ternary blended cement system and late-age strengths (e.g., at 28 days). The 80

following intriguing questions remain unknown: 1) does the more reactive CaCO3 polymorph 81

increase the formation of hemi- or mono- carboaluminate? 2) does the competition for aluminum 82

in metakaolin limit the formation of strätlingite? and 3) does vaterite lead to higher 28-day 83

strengths of VC3 relative to LC3? 84

In this study, we investigated the properties of vaterite and metakaolin-blended Portland 85

cement as the prove-of-concept for the proposed VC3 at a clinker content of ~50%. While 86

applying comparable particle sizes of CaCO3, we examined the mechanical properties, hydration, 87

and microstructure of our VC3 system and compared with those of the classic LC3 system. To 88

verify improved early-age performance, the hydrated VC3 and LC3 (same metakaolin-to-CaCO3 89

mass ratio of 2) at 1-day age were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning 90

electron microscopy (SEM), calorimetry, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The 91

The present work unveils the chemistry and materials properties of the new low-CO2 94

ternary blended system, VC3, and motivates continued studies on VC3 durability and rheology, 95

inspires the development of vaterite-rich blended cement, and provides implications for gigaton- 96

scale enablers of air CO2 capture and storage as well as point source carbon capture and storage. 97

3.1 Flowability and setting time 170

With 15% vaterite (D50 = 5.917 μm) and calcite (D50 = 5.042 μm) particles, the flowability 171

of fresh PLC and PVC pastes was ~0.8 cm lower than that of OPC (Fig.3a) due to the finer 172

consequently high specific surface area, which was 65.7 m2/g for vaterite, compared to 1.3 m2/g 176

for OPC. Compared with PLC, PVC is slightly more flowable due to the presence of vaterite, 177

benefiting from the spherical particles and a larger D50 relative to calcite while partially 178

compromised by the high specific surface area. The flowability of fresh ternary blended cement 179

pastes, LC3 and VC3, with the presence of 0.2% PCE, was ~2 cm lower than that of OPC. It is 180

generally agreed that the high-water demand and flocculation induced by the high specific 181

*Fig.6a shows the 48-h isothermal calorimetry results of fresh pastes, normalized to the 286*

content of Portland cement. Two typical exothermic peaks (C3S hydration at ~7.8 h and C3A at 287

~9.7 h) were observed in OPC, PLC, and PVC [47]. Only one peak before 10 h was observed in 288

LC3 and VC3 as the exothermic peak of C3A merged into the peak of C3S [10], suggesting 289

metakaolin-induced accelerated hydration of C3A [39]. Both calcite and vaterite increased the 290

slope of the acceleration period. Metakaolin further increased the slope of the acceleration period. 291

The above evidences suggest that calcite, vaterite, and metakaolin provided extra nucleation sites 292

to cement hydration [48]. The induction periods of vaterite-blended cements were shorter than 293

those of calcite-blended cements, consistent with the initial setting time results. Existing 294

literature has shown elongated induction periods of MK-blended cements than OPC due to the 295

addition of PCE [49]. However, in the present study, the initial setting of MK-blended cements 296

occurred earlier than that of OPC, supported by the significantly greater slope of its hydration 297

acceleration period compared to OPC. 298

[50]. As Hc was not observed in our XRD result of LC3 at 1 day, and exothermic peak of Hc was 300

emphasize the significance of VC3 that overcomes this disadvantage of LC3 – VC3, without 452

compromising late-age strength, has significantly higher 1-day strength than LC3, suggesting the 453

the mini slump test, no significant difference in flowability between LC3 with VC3 was found. 455

The altered rheology of VC3 is worthy of systematic studies. As the microstructure of hardened 456

paste is refined by vaterite, the potentially improved durability of VC3 requires validation as well. 457

As vaterite is more reactive, the influences of varying calcined clay-CaCO3 ratio deserve equally 458

high attention. 459

The performance enhancement enabled by using vaterite is mainly attributed to its physical 460

(high specific surface and nucleation sites) and chemical (high solubility and reactivity) 461

properties. The physical effect of vaterite is evidenced by the increased hydration rate of clinker 462

due to the high specific surface area (demonstrated by the heat of hydration measurements). The 463

chemical effect is manifested by the increased vaterite reaction degree leading to increased C- 464

(A)-S-H formation (demonstrated with TGA) and by the increased carbonate aluminate 465

generation (demonstrated with QXRD). In addition, the lower density of vaterite relative to 466

calcite corresponds to a greater volume of CaCO3 in VC3 than LC3, resulting in higher degree of 467

CaCO3 consumption in VC3 than in LC3. It is worth noting that VC3 concrete requires slightly 468

lower binder content by mass than LC3 concrete due to the lower density of vaterite and higher 469

strength of VC3. As vaterite reacts faster, the VC3 system may require lower clinker content, 470

further reducing the embodied carbon footprint. The CO2 emissions of calcined clay are ~400 471

kg/ton product [59], while the emissions of vaterite could be nearly neutral or negative 472

depending on the sources of raw materials and manufacturing technology. 473

Vaterite has been widely used as a filler in chemicals or drug carriers in the biomedical 474

industry [60, 61] due to its high specific surface areas, high solubility, high dispersion, and low 475

density [62, 63]. In the construction sector [64], vaterite is used as a key phase in calcium 476

carbonate cement [65], a promising scalable, low-carbon-footprint binder, due to the polymorph 477

transition from vaterite to calcite and/or aragonite. However, the use of calcium carbonate 478

cement, in civil engineering standards, is restricted from wide applications at scale. This fact 479

jeopardizes the research and development of calcium carbonate cement and the 480

commercialization of related entities (e.g., novel cement startups) in the field of climate/clean 481

technology. Compared with LC3, the VC3 system shows higher reactivity and early-age strength. 482

Thus, VC3 could potentially become a superior substitute for LC3 for certain applications. The 483

enhanced performance of the VC3 cementitious system paves a way for large-scale utilization of 484

vaterite and opens a new market for the near-term and long-term operation of the startups. The 485

strategic utilization of vaterite in VC3 could help the startups survive in the capital-intensive 486

construction industry before the approval of calcium carbonate cement for broad applications by 487

national standards and/or before the wide implementation of carbon credit. 488

5. Conclusions 511

We developed and demonstrated a new ternary blended cement system, vaterite calcined 512

clay cement, VC3. 45% of ordinary Portland cement was replaced by metakaolin and metastable 513

CaCO3 polymorph vaterite at a 2:1 blend. Compared to limestone calcined clay cement, LC3, 514

with a similar particle size distribution, VC3 exhibited slightly improved flowability and greatly 515

improved compressive strengths at all ages. With 3% gypsum adjustment, VC3 presents a 13% 516

higher strength relative to ordinary Portland cement reference even at 1 day. The outperformance 517

of VC3 relative to LC3 is explained by the metastability and thus higher reactivity of vaterite 518

relative to calcite. Setting time and heat release measurements demonstrated the faster reaction of 519

vaterite in VC3 than limestone (i.e., calcite) in LC3. XRD results showed that vaterite reacts with 520

metakaolin, forming more hemi- and mono-carboaluminate but less strätlingite than in LC3. TGA 521

results suggested that the formation of AFm phases and pozzolanic reaction largely consumed 522

portlandite. Morphological studies demonstrated that the microstructure of VC3 was refined in 523

the presence of vaterite relative to LC3, where hollow vaterite resulted in higher bulk porosity of 524

VC3 and interior filling with hydration products. 525

Thanks to recent advances in technologies of carbon capture, storage, and utilization (CCUS, 526

also known as clean/climate technologies), vaterite can be massively produced (potentially 100s 527

Mt/year) through carbon mineralization with carbon permanently stored at low costs. Besides 528

vaterite-based cement (e.g., Fortera and Calera), vaterite can be blended to produce VC3 for 529

broader applications. The VC3 system presents a reliable, high-performance complementary 530

product to LC3, particularly when high early-age strengths are required and/or where the LC3 531

productivity is limited by limestone grinding. Therefore, VC3 shows great promises as an enabler 532

of CCUS technologies to mitigate climate change at scale. 533
